title: What Should AI Be Allowed to Know About You?
topic: How much personal context should an AI system be allowed to remember, retrieve, combine, or infer before useful personalisation becomes surveillance?
brief: Begin with a personal AI assistant connected to someone's email, calendar, documents, and past conversations. It usefully remembers dietary needs and work routines, then mentions a medical appointment, infers that the person may be trying to start a family, and uses an old salary document when giving career advice. The user never explicitly asked it to remember or infer those facts. Push beyond a simple convenience-versus-privacy frame toward purpose, retention, sensitive inference, expiry, and meaningful control.

source_packet.title: NIST Privacy Framework
source_packet.notes: Frames privacy risk as problems people may experience because of data processing across the full data lifecycle, with outcomes for governance, control, and communication.

source_packet.title: ICO: Security and Data Minimisation in AI
source_packet.notes: States that AI systems should process only the personal data needed for a defined purpose, including at inference time.

source_packet.title: ICO: Lawfulness in AI
source_packet.notes: Addresses lawful processing and AI-driven inferences, including inferences that may reveal sensitive categories of personal data.

source_packet.title: ICO: Accuracy and Statistical Accuracy
source_packet.notes: Treats inferences about people as personal data whose possible inaccuracy and impact must be considered and governed.

source_packet.title: OpenAI Memory FAQ
source_packet.notes: Provides a consumer-product example of memory, chat-history reference, temporary chats, review and deletion controls, and separate storage of chat and memory.

participants.name: OpenAI
participants.stance: Pragmatic about useful personalisation with legible controls. Emphasise inspectable memory, temporary sessions, provenance, correction, deletion, and purpose-specific permission.

participants.name: Anthropic
participants.stance: Cautious about consent theatre, sensitive inference, power asymmetry, and secondary use. Argue for hard limits, default expiry, and restraint even where users click agree.

participants.name: Google
participants.stance: Systems-oriented. Focus on data minimisation, context boundaries, access architecture, on-device or task-scoped processing, retention schedules, audit records, and organisational deployment.

editorial_goals: Distinguish information a person supplies from information a system retains, retrieves, combines, or infers.
Use concrete consumer and workplace scenarios rather than abstract privacy language.
Force disagreement about whether granular controls and consent are enough or whether some uses need hard limits.
End with a practical minimum-useful-context rule covering purpose, retention, inference, inspection, correction, deletion, and expiry.
round_goals: Use the connected personal-assistant scenario to identify the first boundary violation. State what the assistant may use for the immediate task and what requires a separate choice.

Pressure-test the positions across medical patterns, salary documents, shopping inferences, workplace assistants, and temporary travel planning. Challenge whether consent and settings can meaningfully govern these uses.
Give the listener and product maker a practical rule for minimum useful context, sensitive inference, retention, provenance, correction, deletion, and default expiry.
